title: Normal blood and marrow cells
facts: Which globin genes are on chromosome 16?
The α-globin cluster (ζ and two α genes per chromosome). The β cluster (ε, γ, δ, β) is on chromosome 11.
What is the last dividing stage of the erythroid lineage?
The polychromatic (intermediate) erythroblast.
What is the last dividing stage of the neutrophil lineage?
The myelocyte.
Where are secondary (specific) neutrophil granules first seen?
In the myelocyte.
Name four contents of neutrophil primary granules.
Myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G, defensins (also proteinase 3 and lysozyme).
What is the normal adult HbA2 level?
What is the normal adult P50?
About 26.6 mmHg (3.5 kPa).
Name four causes of a right-shifted oxygen dissociation curve.
Acidosis, raised CO2, fever, raised 2,3-BPG.
Why is the fetal dissociation curve left-shifted?
HbF (α2γ2) binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its oxygen affinity is higher; P50 about 19 mmHg.
Which enzyme makes NADPH in the red cell?
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, in the hexose monophosphate shunt.
Where is erythropoietin mainly produced?
Peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex (about 90%); the rest in the liver.
How is thrombopoietin regulated?
It is made at a constant rate by the liver and cleared by binding MPL on platelets and megakaryocytes, so the free level falls as platelet mass rises.
What is the phenotype of the haematopoietic stem cell?
CD34+, CD38−, CD90+, CD45RA−, lineage-negative.
Which axis keeps stem cells in the marrow, and which drug blocks it?
CXCL12 (SDF-1) binding CXCR4. Plerixafor blocks CXCR4 to mobilise stem cells.
What is the blood half-life of a neutrophil?
About 6 to 7 hours.
Which defect causes chronic granulomatous disease?
Defective NADPH oxidase, so no respiratory burst.
Which defect causes leucocyte adhesion deficiency type 1?
Deficiency of CD18, the common β2 integrin chain.
Which cytokine drives eosinophil production?
IL-5.
How do you tell a basophil from a mast cell by flow cytometry?
Basophils are CD123+ CD203c+ and CD117−; mast cells are CD117 (bright)+ and tryptase+.
What is the CD4:CD8 ratio in normal blood?
About 2:1.
What phenotype distinguishes normal plasma cells from myeloma cells?
Normal plasma cells are CD19+ and CD56−. Myeloma cells are usually CD19− and often CD56+, and are light-chain restricted.
What is a ring sideroblast?
An erythroblast with 5 or more siderotic granules covering at least one third of the nuclear circumference.
What proportion of normal erythroblasts are sideroblasts?
About 20% to 50%.
What is the normal adult M:E ratio?
About 2:1 to 4:1.
How many cells should a marrow differential count?
At least 500 nucleated cells, ideally from two films.
What is the minimum adequate trephine length?
At least 1.5–2 cm of marrow (ICSH and BSH guidance).
Where do normal megakaryocytes lie in a trephine section?
Next to sinusoids in the intertrabecular space, away from bone. Paratrabecular megakaryocytes or tight clusters are abnormal.
What ploidy do most megakaryocytes reach?
16N (range 8N to 64N), by endomitosis.
How long do platelets survive?
7 to 10 days.
What fraction of platelets is pooled in the spleen?
About one third.
Which glycoprotein is defective in Glanzmann thrombasthenia?
GPIIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3), the fibrinogen receptor.
Which glycoprotein is defective in Bernard–Soulier syndrome?
GPIb–IX–V, the VWF receptor.
What do dense granules contain?
ADP, ATP, serotonin and calcium.
What is the haemoglobin cut-off for anaemia in pregnancy?
110 g/L (WHO).
When is the physiological haemoglobin nadir in term infants?
At about 8 to 12 weeks, around 95–110 g/L.
What neutrophil count can be normal in Duffy-null individuals?
What is the formula for MCHC?
MCHC = Hb ÷ Hct. Normal 315–345 g/L.
How do you correct a white cell count for nucleated red cells?
Corrected WBC = measured WBC × 100 ÷ (100 + NRBC per 100 WBC). Most modern analysers do this automatically.
What causes EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia?
Antibodies against a GPIIb/IIIa epitope exposed by calcium chelation, which clump platelets in vitro. Repeat in citrate or examine a film.
What is the reticulin grade of normal marrow?
MF-0 to MF-1.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old has a marrow aspirate with no particles, few myeloid precursors, many segmented neutrophils and an M:E ratio of 12:1. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Haemodilution of the aspirate with peripheral blood
quiz.e: An aspirate without particles whose differential looks like blood (mature neutrophils and lymphocytes, few precursors) is haemodiluted. Interpret cellularity on the trephine and repeat the aspirate if needed.

quiz.q: Which stage of neutrophil maturation is the last one able to divide?
quiz.e: Myeloblast, promyelocyte and myelocyte form the mitotic pool. From the metamyelocyte onwards, the cells only mature.

quiz.q: Which finding best distinguishes an osteoclast from a megakaryocyte on an aspirate?
o: Multiple separate nuclei rather than one lobulated nucleus
quiz.e: Both are giant cells with granular cytoplasm. The osteoclast has many separate round nuclei, each with a nucleolus; the megakaryocyte has one lobulated polyploid nucleus.

quiz.q: Which of the following shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left?
quiz.e: HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, which raises oxygen affinity and lowers P50 to about 19 mmHg. The other three shift the curve to the right.

quiz.q: In a normal adult, HbA2 accounts for about:
quiz.e: HbA2 (α2δ2) is 2.2% to 3.5%. A raised HbA2 is the key screening finding in β-thalassaemia trait, which Module 2 covers.

quiz.q: A ring sideroblast is defined as an erythroblast with:
o: At least 3 granules anywhere in the cytoplasm
At least 5 granules covering one third or more of the nuclear rim
Granules covering the entire nuclear rim
quiz.e: WHO and ICSH define a ring sideroblast as having 5 or more granules covering at least one third of the nuclear circumference.

quiz.q: Which immunophenotype describes a normal haematopoietic stem cell?
quiz.e: The most primitive cells are CD34+ CD38− CD90+ CD45RA− and lineage-negative. CD34+ CD10+ CD19+ describes an early B cell precursor (hematogone stage I).

quiz.q: A healthy 2-year-old has a lymphocyte count of 6.5 × 10⁹/L and a normal film. What is the best interpretation?
o: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia until proven otherwise
quiz.e: Lymphocytes predominate in young children, and counts up to about 9–10 × 10⁹/L are within the reference range at age 2. Always use age-specific ranges.

quiz.q: Which marker pair best separates basophils from mast cells on flow cytometry?
o: CD117 and tryptase are positive in basophils
CD34 is positive in mast cells
quiz.e: Basophils are CD123+ CD203c+ and CD117−. Mast cells are CD117 bright and tryptase positive.

quiz.q: Where are megakaryocytes normally located in a trephine biopsy?
o: Next to sinusoids in the intertrabecular space
quiz.e: Megakaryocytes release proplatelets into sinusoids, so they sit next to them. Paratrabecular megakaryocytes and tight clusters are features of myeloproliferative neoplasms.

quiz.q: Which enzyme deficiency leaves the red cell vulnerable to oxidant damage?
quiz.e: G6PD produces NADPH in the hexose monophosphate shunt, which keeps glutathione reduced. Cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency causes methaemoglobinaemia instead.

quiz.q: A count of 40 × 10⁹/L platelets is reported on an EDTA sample from a well patient with no bleeding. The analyser flags platelet clumps. What is the best next step?
o: Examine the film and repeat the count on a citrate sample
quiz.e: This suggests EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia. Confirm clumps on the film and recount in citrate (correcting for dilution) or from a fingerprick sample.

quiz.q: Which growth factor is made at a constant rate and regulated mainly by its clearance?
quiz.e: The liver makes TPO constitutively. Platelets and megakaryocytes bind and remove it through MPL, so free TPO falls as platelet mass rises.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of the fall in haemoglobin during normal pregnancy?
o: Plasma volume expanding more than red cell mass
quiz.e: Plasma volume rises by 40–50% and red cell mass by only 20–30%, giving a dilutional fall. Iron deficiency is common too, but it is not the physiological mechanism.

quiz.q: An analyser reports MCHC 390 g/L, MCV 112 fL and a low red cell count, and the sample was taken on a cold morning. What should you do first?
o: Warm the sample to 37°C and repeat
quiz.e: Red cell agglutinates are counted as single large cells, so the red cell count falls and MCV and MCHC rise falsely. Warming disperses a cold agglutinin.

quiz.q: Which feature of the plasma cell is described as 'clock-face'?
o: The chromatin arranged in coarse clumps around the nucleus
The shape of the Golgi zone
quiz.e: Clumps of heterochromatin around the nuclear rim resemble the numbers on a clock face.

quiz.q: Normal marrow cellularity in a 70-year-old is closest to:
quiz.e: Using 100 minus age as a rough guide gives about 30%. Ignore the subcortical spaces, which are often hypocellular.

quiz.q: Which of these is a normal finding in a bone marrow aspirate?
quiz.e: Emperipolesis, where marrow cells pass through megakaryocyte cytoplasm, is normal. It can be increased in some myeloproliferative neoplasms.

steps.q: What is your first step?
o: Postpone surgery and refer to haematology
Examine the blood film from the same EDTA sample
steps.e: A low platelet count in a well patient with no bleeding history and a clump flag should be checked on the film before anything else.
steps.scene:
A 46-year-old woman attends for a routine pre-operative check before a hernia repair. She has no bleeding history and no bruising. Her full blood count is otherwise normal.
Hb 134 g/L · WBC 6.8 × 10⁹/L · Platelets 38 × 10⁹/L · MPV Not reported · Analyser flag PLT clumps?

steps.q: The film shows large platelet clumps at the feathered edge, and some neutrophils ringed by platelets. What is the most likely explanation?
steps.e: EDTA exposes a cryptic GPIIb/IIIa epitope that some people's antibodies (about 0.1% of the population) recognise. Platelets clump in the tube and may stick to neutrophils (satellitism).

steps.q: How do you get a reliable count?
o: Repeat on a sodium citrate sample, analysed promptly and corrected for dilution
steps.e:
Citrate prevents the clumping in most cases. Multiply the count by about 1.1 to correct for the liquid anticoagulant. A fingerprick film or a sample kept at 37°C are alternatives.
Take-home: Always look at the film before reporting an unexpected thrombocytopenia; EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia has no clinical significance, but missing it leads to needless transfusion or cancelled surgery; Record the finding in the patient's file so future counts are interpreted correctly.

steps.q: Which value is physiologically impossible?
steps.e: An MCHC above about 370 g/L cannot occur in intact red cells, because haemoglobin would crystallise. It points to an artefact in the red cell count or haematocrit.
steps.scene:
A 72-year-old man is seen with tiredness. His sample was taken in a cold clinic in winter and arrived in the laboratory two hours later.
Hb 118 g/L · RBC 2.10 × 10¹²/L · Hct 0.24 L/L · MCV 114 fL · MCH 56 pg · MCHC 492 g/L

steps.q: How does a cold agglutinin produce this pattern?
o: It lyses red cells in the tube
Agglutinated red cells are counted as single large cells, so RBC and Hct fall while Hb, measured after lysis, is correct
steps.e: Haemoglobin is measured after lysis, so it stays correct. The red cell count and haematocrit fall, which makes MCH and MCHC rise falsely, and doublets raise the MCV.

steps.q: What is the correct action?
o: Report the results with a comment
Warm the sample to 37°C for 15 to 30 minutes and rerun it at once
Request a new EDTA sample at room temperature
steps.e:
Warming disperses the agglutinates. If the problem persists, take a new sample kept at 37°C. The film shows red cell agglutinates. Then think about the cause (Module 2 covers cold agglutinin disease).
Take-home: MCHC is the best internal quality check on red cell indices; Raised MCHC: cold agglutinin, lipaemia, icterus and hereditary spherocytosis (rarely above 370 g/L); Lipaemia falsely raises Hb; it is corrected by plasma replacement.

cases.title: An aspirate that looks like blood

steps.q: What best explains this differential count?
o: Haemodilution of the aspirate with peripheral blood
steps.e: No particles, very few precursors and a differential count resembling blood means the aspirate is mostly peripheral blood. The M:E ratio cannot be interpreted.
steps.scene:
A 58-year-old man has a bone marrow aspirate and trephine to investigate mild pancytopenia. The operator reports that aspiration was difficult. The trephine report is pending.
Particles None seen · Blasts 1% · Myelocytes and metamyelocytes 6% · Segmented neutrophils 52% · Lymphocytes 28% · Erythroblasts 5% · M:E ratio about 12:1

steps.q: Why might the aspiration have been difficult?
o: Marrow fibrosis or very cellular, packed marrow
steps.e: A dry or blood-only tap can come from technique, but it raises the possibility of fibrosis, infiltration (for example hairy cell leukaemia or metastases) or a packed marrow. The trephine is essential.

steps.q: What should the report say?
o: Aspirate haemodiluted and not representative; interpret together with the trephine, which may need imprints
steps.e:
State that the aspirate is not representative. Trephine touch imprints give cytology when aspiration fails, and the reticulin stain assesses fibrosis.
Take-home: Assess particles before interpreting any aspirate count; Never call a marrow hypocellular from a haemodiluted aspirate; A dry tap is a clue to fibrosis or infiltration until proven otherwise.

steps.q: How should the haemoglobin be interpreted?
o: Anaemia by WHO criteria; check iron status
steps.e: Haemoglobin below 110 g/L is anaemia in pregnancy (below 105 g/L in the second trimester by UK guidance). Iron deficiency is the commonest cause, so check ferritin even with a normal MCV, since MCV rises a little in pregnancy.
steps.scene:
A 29-year-old woman at 34 weeks of an uncomplicated pregnancy has a routine blood count. She feels well and has no bleeding.
Hb 106 g/L · MCV 92 fL · WBC 13.2 × 10⁹/L · Neutrophils 10.1 × 10⁹/L · Film Occasional myelocytes · Platelets 118 × 10⁹/L

steps.q: How should the white count be interpreted?
o: Normal pregnancy neutrophilia with a mild left shift
steps.e: Neutrophilia with occasional myelocytes is normal in pregnancy. Clinical signs, not the count alone, decide whether infection is present.

steps.q: What is the most likely cause of the platelet count?
steps.e:
A mild fall late in pregnancy in a well woman with a normal blood pressure and a platelet count above 70 × 10⁹/L is most often gestational. Check blood pressure and liver tests to exclude pre-eclampsia and HELLP.
Take-home: Use pregnancy-specific ranges; Plasma volume expands more than red cell mass; Neutrophilia with left shift and mild thrombocytopenia are expected in the third trimester.

trees.title: A result that looks wrong
trees.intro: Follow the questions to the most likely artefact.

opts: White count raised, film shows nucleated red cells
MCV and Hct rising, sample is old

plt.q: Is the patient well, with no bleeding, and is there a clump flag?

plt2.q: Does the film show platelet clumps or satellitism?

pltedta.detail: Recount on a citrate sample (multiply by about 1.1) or a fingerprick film. Add a comment to the report and the patient record.

pltclot.q: Is there a visible clot or fibrin strands in the tube?

pltclot2.detail: Reject the sample and request a new one with a clean venepuncture and prompt mixing.

pltreal.detail: Confirm on the film, review platelet size and other cell lines, and investigate the cause (Module 4).

mchc.q: Is the plasma milky (lipaemic) or deeply icteric?

lip.detail: Turbidity raises Hb, so MCH and MCHC rise. Replace the plasma with an equal volume of diluent and rerun, or measure Hb by another method.

cold.q: Does the film or the tube show red cell agglutinates?

coldagg.detail: Warm to 37°C and rerun at once. Then look for the cause: cold agglutinin disease, Mycoplasma, EBV or lymphoma.

hs.end: Consider hereditary spherocytosis, or a sample artefact
hs.detail: Look for spherocytes on the film. True MCHC rarely exceeds 370 g/L. Recheck the instrument and quality control.

nrbc.q: Does your analyser count nucleated red cells separately?

nrbcauto.end: Use the analyser's corrected white count
nrbcauto.detail: Check that the reported WBC is the corrected value. Then interpret the NRBCs: neonate, haemolysis, hypoxia, marrow infiltration (leucoerythroblastic film).

nrbccalc.detail: Corrected WBC = WBC × 100 ÷ (100 + NRBC per 100 WBC). Use the calculator below.

old.q: Was the sample stored at room temperature for more than about 24 hours?

oldyes.detail: Red cells swell, so MCV and Hct rise while MCHC falls. Films show crenation and degenerating neutrophils. Request a fresh sample.

oldno.detail: Check the film for oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils and investigate (Module 2).

check.title: Reporting a bone marrow aspirate
check.intro: A systematic order for reading an aspirate. Tick each step as you go.
steps: Check the request
Read the clinical question and the blood count taken within 24 hours of the marrow. Write down what you need to answer.
Low power: is it adequate?
Look for particles and their cellularity. If there are no particles, say the aspirate may be haemodiluted.
Low power: megakaryocytes
Present, reduced or increased? Note size, lobulation and any clustering.
Low power: abnormal cells
Scan for clumps of non-haematopoietic cells (metastases), giant cells and granulomas.
High power: differential
Count at least 500 cells in the trails behind particles. Calculate the M:E ratio.
Each lineage in turn
Erythroid: maturation, megaloblastic or dysplastic change. Myeloid: blast %, maturation, granulation, Auer rods. Lymphoid and plasma cells: proportion and morphology.
Iron stain
Grade storage iron in particles, count sideroblasts and look for ring sideroblasts.
Correlate
Compare with the trephine (cellularity, fibrosis, focal lesions), flow cytometry and genetics.
Write the conclusion
Answer the clinical question in the first line. List the key findings and any recommended further tests.

title: Red cell disorders
facts: What are the WHO haemoglobin cut-offs for anaemia?
Men 130 g/L, non-pregnant women 120 g/L, pregnancy 110 g/L.
What does hepcidin do?
It binds ferroportin and causes its degradation, blocking iron export from enterocytes and macrophages.
Which cytokine raises hepcidin in inflammation?
IL-6.
Which hormone from erythroblasts suppresses hepcidin?
Erythroferrone.
What ferritin is diagnostic of iron deficiency?
Below 15 µg/L; many guidelines use below 30 µg/L.
Which gene is mutated in IRIDA?
TMPRSS6 (matriptase-2), giving inappropriately high hepcidin.
Where is vitamin B12 absorbed?
In the terminal ileum, bound to intrinsic factor, through the cubam receptor.
Which metabolite rises in B12 but not folate deficiency?
Methylmalonic acid.
Define neutrophil hypersegmentation.
5% or more of neutrophils with 5 lobes, or any neutrophil with 6 or more lobes.
Why replace B12 before folate?
Folate alone can correct the anaemia but worsen B12 neuropathy (subacute combined degeneration).
Which antibody test is most specific for pernicious anaemia?
Intrinsic factor antibody (about 50% sensitive).
Name the haemolysis markers.
Raised reticulocytes, unconjugated bilirubin and LDH; low haptoglobin.
What is the preferred screening test for hereditary spherocytosis?
The EMA binding test by flow cytometry (reduced fluorescence).
Which protein is most often defective in hereditary spherocytosis?
Ankyrin.
In which membrane disorder is splenectomy contraindicated?
Hereditary stomatocytosis and xerocytosis, because of thrombosis risk.
How is G6PD deficiency inherited?
X-linked.
Why can a G6PD assay be falsely normal after a crisis?
Young red cells and reticulocytes have higher enzyme activity. Repeat about 3 months later.
Name four drugs to avoid in G6PD deficiency.
Primaquine (and tafenoquine), dapsone, rasburicase, nitrofurantoin; also sulfonamides and methylene blue.
Why do patients with PK deficiency tolerate anaemia well?
2,3-BPG accumulates and right-shifts the oxygen dissociation curve.
What causes prominent basophilic stippling?
Lead poisoning, P5'N deficiency, thalassaemia, dyserythropoiesis.
What α-globin genotype gives HbH disease?
Three genes deleted: −−/−α.
What HbA2 level suggests β-thalassaemia trait?
Above 3.5% (often 4% to 6%).
What can mask β-thalassaemia trait?
Coexisting iron deficiency, which lowers HbA2.
What is the Mentzer index?
MCV ÷ RBC count. Under 13 suggests thalassaemia trait, over 13 iron deficiency (screening only).
What is the mutation in HbS?
β6 glutamic acid to valine.
What is the mutation in HbC?
β6 glutamic acid to lysine.
What does the sickle solubility test miss?
It cannot tell trait from disease, and is unreliable under about 6 months of age.
What is the DAT pattern in warm AIHA?
IgG, with or without C3d.
What is the DAT pattern in cold agglutinin disease?
C3d only.
What is the Donath–Landsteiner antibody?
A biphasic IgG with anti-P specificity, causing paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria.
What fragment count is significant in adults?
Over 1% of red cells (ICSH).
What ADAMTS13 level supports TTP?
Below 10% activity.
What is the defect in PNH?
An acquired PIGA mutation; no GPI anchors, so CD55 and CD59 are lost.
How is PNH best diagnosed?
High-sensitivity flow cytometry with FLAER on neutrophils and monocytes.
What are the Camitta criteria for severe aplastic anaemia?
Cellularity under 25% plus two of: neutrophils under 0.5, platelets under 20, reticulocytes under 20 × 10⁹/L.
Which test diagnoses Fanconi anaemia?
Chromosome breakage with diepoxybutane (DEB) or mitomycin C.
What marrow cell suggests parvovirus B19?
The giant pronormoblast.
Name causes of acquired sideroblastic anaemia.
Alcohol, isoniazid, lead, copper deficiency (zinc excess), MDS with SF3B1 mutation.
Which gene causes X-linked sideroblastic anaemia?
ALAS2.
Which CDA shows binucleate erythroblasts?
CDA II (SEC23B), formerly HEMPAS.

quiz.q: A 34-year-old woman has Hb 98 g/L, MCV 68 fL, RBC 4.2 × 10¹²/L, RDW 18%, platelets 480 × 10⁹/L and ferritin 6 µg/L. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.e: A very low ferritin is diagnostic. The high RDW, low RBC count and reactive thrombocytosis all fit.

quiz.q: Hb 128 g/L, MCV 62 fL, RBC 6.1 × 10¹²/L, RDW 13.5%, ferritin 85 µg/L. What is the most useful next test?
quiz.e: Marked microcytosis with a high RBC count, normal RDW and normal ferritin suggest thalassaemia trait. The Mentzer index is about 10. HPLC quantifies HbA2.

quiz.q: Which result best distinguishes iron deficiency from anaemia of inflammation?
quiz.e: Serum iron and transferrin saturation fall in both. Soluble transferrin receptor rises with iron-deficient erythropoiesis but stays normal in inflammation.

quiz.q: A patient with megaloblastic anaemia has a raised methylmalonic acid and raised homocysteine. What is the deficiency?
quiz.e: Methylmalonic acid rises only in B12 deficiency, because B12 is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Homocysteine rises in both.

quiz.q: Which finding on the film is the earliest and most specific clue to megaloblastic anaemia?
quiz.e: Hypersegmented neutrophils can appear before macrocytosis or anaemia.

quiz.q: A child has anaemia, splenomegaly, spherocytes, MCHC 368 g/L and a negative DAT. Which test is preferred to confirm the diagnosis?
quiz.e: EMA binding has high sensitivity and specificity for hereditary spherocytosis and is the preferred screening test. The negative DAT excludes immune spherocytosis.

quiz.q: Two days after starting primaquine, a man develops dark urine and anaemia. The film shows bite and blister cells. His G6PD assay is normal. What next?
o: Repeat the G6PD assay about 3 months after recovery
quiz.e: After acute haemolysis, the surviving young red cells have more G6PD, which can give a falsely normal result.

quiz.q: Hb 92 g/L, MCV 64 fL, HbA2 2.4%, normal ferritin, and golf-ball inclusions on brilliant cresyl blue. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.e: HbH inclusions (β4 tetramers) in a microcytic anaemia with normal or low HbA2 mean HbH disease: 3 of 4 α genes deleted.

quiz.q: A woman with iron deficiency anaemia has HbA2 3.2%. Her partner has β-thalassaemia trait. What is the best advice?
o: Repeat HbA2 after iron is replaced
quiz.e: Iron deficiency lowers HbA2 and can mask β-thalassaemia trait. This matters for reproductive counselling.

quiz.q: A sickle solubility test is positive. Which statement is correct?
o: The patient has sickle cell disease
The patient has sickle cell trait
HbS is present, but trait cannot be told from disease
The test is diagnostic in newborns
quiz.e: A positive solubility test means HbS is present. HPLC or electrophoresis quantifies it and separates trait (about 35–40% HbS) from disease.

quiz.q: Haemolytic anaemia with spherocytes and a DAT positive for IgG and C3d, in a 70-year-old with lymphocytosis. What is the most likely underlying cause?
quiz.e: Warm AIHA is a well-known complication of CLL. Hereditary spherocytosis is DAT-negative.

quiz.q: A DAT positive for C3d only, red cell agglutination on the film and acrocyanosis in winter. What is the antibody?
quiz.e: Cold agglutinins are IgM and fix complement, so only C3d stays on the cells at 37°C.

quiz.q: Thrombocytopenia 18 × 10⁹/L, schistocytes 4%, LDH 1900 U/L, mild confusion and normal clotting times. What is the urgent test?
o: ADAMTS13 activity, while starting plasma exchange
quiz.e: This is suspected TTP. Treatment must not wait for the result. ADAMTS13 below 10% confirms it.

quiz.q: Which test is preferred to diagnose PNH?
o: Flow cytometry with FLAER on neutrophils and monocytes
quiz.e: High-sensitivity flow cytometry of white cells is the standard. Red cell clones are underestimated after haemolysis or transfusion.

quiz.q: A child with hereditary spherocytosis suddenly becomes very pale. Hb 45 g/L and reticulocytes 0.1%. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.e: Parvovirus B19 halts erythropoiesis. With a shortened red cell lifespan, haemoglobin falls fast, and reticulocytes are absent.

quiz.q: Which marrow finding defines a ring sideroblast?
o: 5 or more granules covering one third or more of the nuclear rim
quiz.e: This is the WHO and ICSH definition. Normal sideroblasts have a few scattered granules.

quiz.q: Pancytopenia, marrow cellularity 10%, neutrophils 0.15 × 10⁹/L, platelets 8 × 10⁹/L, reticulocytes 12 × 10⁹/L. How is it classified?
quiz.e: Severe criteria are met, and neutrophils below 0.2 × 10⁹/L make it very severe.

quiz.q: A young man with microcytic anaemia, abdominal pain and coarse basophilic stippling works in battery recycling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.e: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase and P5'N, giving stippling and sometimes ring sideroblasts.

steps.q: What is the most likely cause of the microcytosis?
steps.e: Marked microcytosis with a high RBC count, normal RDW and normal ferritin points to thalassaemia trait. Mentzer index: 66 ÷ 5.4 ≈ 12.
steps.scene:
A 26-year-old woman at 12 weeks of pregnancy has a routine blood count. Her partner's family is from Cyprus.
Hb 104 g/L · MCV 66 fL · MCH 20 pg · RBC 5.4 × 10¹²/L · RDW 13.8% · Ferritin 64 µg/L

steps.q: HPLC shows HbA2 5.1% and HbF 1.2%. What does this mean?
steps.e: HbA2 above 3.5% confirms β-thalassaemia trait.

steps.q: What is the most important next step?
steps.e:
If the partner is also a carrier, the fetus has a 1 in 4 risk of β-thalassaemia major. Offer prenatal diagnosis early.
Take-home: Microcytosis with a normal ferritin needs haemoglobin studies; Antenatal screening is time-critical: test the partner straight away; Do not give iron empirically to thalassaemia carriers who are iron-replete.

steps.q: Which film finding would you most expect?
o: Teardrop cells and nucleated red cells only
steps.e: Megaloblastic anaemia gives oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Pancytopenia and a very high LDH reflect ineffective haematopoiesis.
steps.scene:
A 62-year-old woman has 4 months of fatigue and pins and needles in both feet. She has hypothyroidism.
Hb 78 g/L · MCV 121 fL · WBC 3.1 × 10⁹/L · Platelets 96 × 10⁹/L · Retics 22 × 10⁹/L · LDH 2400 U/L

steps.q: Serum B12 is low. Which test best supports pernicious anaemia?
steps.e: Intrinsic factor antibodies are highly specific. Parietal cell antibodies are sensitive but found in many older people without the disease.

steps.q: How should she be treated?
o: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin, with folate only once B12 is started
steps.e:
She has neurological symptoms, so start IM hydroxocobalamin promptly. Never give folate alone. Watch potassium and iron as the marrow recovers.
Take-home: Autoimmune thyroid disease is associated with pernicious anaemia; Neurological symptoms can occur without anaemia; Reticulocytes peak at about day 5 to 7 after B12 treatment.

cases.title: Dark urine after a bean meal

steps.q: Which film finding supports the likely diagnosis?
o: Bite cells, blister cells and irregularly contracted cells
steps.e: Oxidant haemolysis in G6PD deficiency produces bite and blister cells. Supravital staining shows Heinz bodies.
steps.scene:
A 7-year-old boy from Egypt is brought in with pallor, jaundice and cola-coloured urine, 2 days after eating fresh fava beans.
Hb 68 g/L · Retics 9% · Bilirubin 62 µmol/L (unconj.) · LDH 1650 U/L · Haptoglobin Undetectable · DAT Negative

steps.q: A G6PD screening test now is normal. How do you interpret it?
o: May be falsely normal because of reticulocytosis; repeat after about 3 months
steps.e: Young red cells carry more enzyme. Either repeat later or compare the result with the reticulocyte count.

steps.q: What is the key long-term advice?
o: Avoid fava beans and oxidant drugs; carry a list
steps.e:
Avoiding triggers prevents most episodes. Give the family a written list of unsafe drugs.
Take-home: Haemolysis plus a negative DAT plus bite cells: think G6PD; X-linked: boys are most affected; Rasburicase and primaquine need G6PD testing first.

steps.q: What test do you request next?
steps.e: Spherocytes with haemolysis in an older adult with lymphocytosis point to warm AIHA. The DAT is the key test.
steps.scene:
A 71-year-old man presents with breathlessness and jaundice. He was told of 'a high white count' two years ago.
Hb 64 g/L · WBC 48 × 10⁹/L · Lymphocytes 44 × 10⁹/L · Retics 310 × 10⁹/L · Bilirubin 48 µmol/L · Film Spherocytes, smear cells

steps.q: DAT: IgG positive, C3d weakly positive. What is the most likely underlying disease?
steps.e: Smear cells and a mature lymphocytosis suggest CLL, confirmed by flow cytometry (Module 3). AIHA occurs in about 5% to 10% of CLL.

steps.q: What should the transfusion laboratory be told?
o: Autoantibody present: it may mask alloantibodies, so extended testing is needed before transfusion
Give group O negative blood only
steps.e:
Panreactive autoantibodies make crossmatching harder. Adsorption studies exclude underlying alloantibodies. Do not withhold life-saving transfusion.
Take-home: Warm AIHA: IgG ± C3d, spherocytes; Look for an underlying cause: CLL, lymphoma, SLE, drugs; Communicate early with the blood bank.

steps.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.e: MAHA with severe thrombocytopenia, neurological signs and normal clotting points to TTP. DIC would prolong the clotting times.
steps.scene:
A 38-year-old woman has 3 days of headache, purpura and new confusion. Blood pressure is normal.
Hb 82 g/L · Platelets 14 × 10⁹/L · Schistocytes 5% · LDH 1800 U/L · PT / APTT Normal · Creatinine 118 µmol/L

steps.q: What do you do now?
o: Start plasma exchange urgently, after taking a sample for ADAMTS13
steps.e: Untreated TTP is often fatal. Take the sample before plasma exchange, but do not delay treatment. Avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding is life-threatening.

steps.q: ADAMTS13 activity is under 5% with an inhibitor. What does this confirm?
steps.e:
An anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibody defines immune TTP. Treatment adds steroids, rituximab and caplacizumab to plasma exchange.
Take-home: Count schistocytes when thrombocytopenia and haemolysis coexist; TTP is a haematological emergency; The PLASMIC score helps while ADAMTS13 is pending.

trees.title: Anaemia algorithm
trees.intro: Start with any anaemia. Each step uses a result you would have on the first day.

start.q: Reticulocyte response: is the absolute reticulocyte count raised (RPI 2 or more)?

bleed.end: Blood loss with an appropriate marrow response
bleed.detail: Find and stop the source. Iron deficiency will follow if bleeding continues.

haemol.detail: Confirm with bilirubin, LDH and haptoglobin, then follow the haemolysis tree.

ida.detail: Find the cause: menstrual loss, GI loss (investigate men and postmenopausal women), malabsorption (coeliac), diet.

micro2.q: Is there evidence of inflammation (high CRP, chronic disease) and a low TSAT?

acd.detail: A ferritin up to about 100 µg/L with TSAT under 20% can still hide iron deficiency. Soluble transferrin receptor helps.

thal.end: Consider thalassaemia trait or sideroblastic anaemia
thal.detail: High RBC count and normal RDW favour thalassaemia: do HPLC. A dimorphic film or high ferritin: do a marrow with Perls stain.

normo.q: Are other lineages abnormal, or is the film leucoerythroblastic?

marrow.detail: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine: aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, myeloma, metastases, fibrosis.

normo2.q: Is there chronic kidney disease, inflammation or endocrine disease?

secondary.end: Anaemia of CKD, inflammation or endocrine disease
secondary.detail: Check eGFR, CRP, thyroid function. In CKD the anaemia reflects inadequate EPO.

mixed.end: Look for early or mixed deficiency
mixed.detail: A high RDW suggests mixed iron and B12 or folate deficiency. Check haematinics and the film. Consider pure red cell aplasia if retics are near zero.

macro.q: Does the film show oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils?

mega.detail: B12 and folate (± MMA, holoTC), intrinsic factor antibodies. Check drugs. Give B12 before or with folate.

nonmega.detail: Alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, drugs, reticulocytosis. If cytopenias or dysplasia are present: marrow for MDS.

trees.title: Haemolysis workup
trees.intro: Use once haemolysis is confirmed (raised reticulocytes, bilirubin and LDH; low haptoglobin).

warm.detail: Spherocytes. Look for CLL, lymphoma, SLE, drugs. Check recent transfusion or pregnancy for alloimmune causes.

cold.q: Is there red cell agglutination, or a high-titre cold agglutinin?
opts: No, acute haemoglobinuria in a child

cad.detail: Primary (clonal B cell) or secondary to Mycoplasma, EBV or lymphoma. Warm samples before counting.

pch.detail: Do the Donath–Landsteiner test. Note that the DAT can be positive for C3d only.

maha.detail: Urgent: clotting screen, ADAMTS13 (TTP), renal function and stool culture (HUS), BP and pregnancy status.

hs.detail: EMA binding test, family history. Exclude DAT-negative AIHA and burns or Clostridium sepsis in the right setting.

g6pd.detail: G6PD assay (may be falsely normal just after a crisis). Supravital stain for Heinz bodies; consider unstable haemoglobin.

hb.detail: HPLC or capillary electrophoresis, sickle solubility test, family studies.

other.q: Is there intravascular haemolysis, thrombosis or cytopenia?

pnh.detail: High-sensitivity flow cytometry: FLAER on neutrophils and monocytes, CD59 on red cells.

enz.end: Consider PK deficiency or another enzymopathy
enz.detail: Red cell enzyme panel (PK, P5'N), membrane studies, and an NGS gene panel if unresolved.

check.title: Reporting a red cell film
check.intro: A systematic order for describing red cells on a blood film. Tick each step as you go.
steps: Choose the right area
The thin area where red cells just touch. Thick areas hide pallor; the feathered edge distorts shapes.
Size
Compare with a small lymphocyte nucleus. Normocytic, microcytic, macrocytic, or dimorphic (two populations).
Colour
Normochromic or hypochromic. Polychromasia (reticulocytes). Spherocytes have no pallor.
Shape (poikilocytes)
Name each type present and grade it: spherocytes, target cells, elliptocytes, fragments, sickle cells, teardrops, acanthocytes, echinocytes, stomatocytes, bite and blister cells.
Inclusions
Howell–Jolly bodies, basophilic stippling, Pappenheimer bodies, parasites, nucleated red cells.
Arrangement
Rouleaux or agglutination.
White cells and platelets
Hypersegmented neutrophils, blasts, leucoerythroblastic picture, platelet number and size.
Conclusion
One sentence with the most likely cause, and the tests that would confirm it (for example, ferritin, HPLC, DAT, EMA, G6PD).

title: White cell disorders and leukaemia
facts: Which features favour a leukaemoid reaction over CML?
Toxic granulation, no basophilia, neutrophils and bands dominating, normal spleen, BCR::ABL1 negative.
What is a Döhle body?
A pale blue patch of rough endoplasmic reticulum at the edge of a neutrophil; seen in infection and May–Hegglin anomaly.
What does a leucoerythroblastic film suggest?
Marrow infiltration or fibrosis (also severe stress or haemorrhage).
Which antigen is brightest on lymphocytes and absent from red cell precursors?
CD45.
Where do blasts fall on a CD45/SSC plot?
CD45 dim, low to intermediate side scatter.
What is the lineage-defining marker for T lineage?
Cytoplasmic (or surface) CD3.
What defines myeloid lineage in MPAL?
MPO positivity, or monocytic differentiation with two or more of NSE, CD11c, CD14, CD64 and lysozyme.
What κ:λ ratio suggests a clonal B-cell population?
Above about 3:1 or below about 1:2 (or absent surface light chain).
Which cells count as blast equivalents in AML?
Promonocytes, and abnormal promyelocytes in APL.
In WHO-HAEM5, which AML genetic types still need 20% blasts?
AML with BCR::ABL1 and AML with CEBPA mutation.
What blast threshold does ICC use for AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities?
10% (20% for BCR::ABL1).
What is MDS/AML in ICC 2022?
A myeloid neoplasm with 10–19% blasts and no AML-defining genetic abnormality.
How is AML-MR defined in WHO-HAEM5?
20% or more blasts with myelodysplasia-related cytogenetics or mutations in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1 or ZRSR2.
What is the typical phenotype of APL?
CD34−, HLA-DR−, CD33 bright, CD117+, CD11b−, MPO strong.
What is the first treatment step when APL is suspected?
Start ATRA immediately and correct the coagulopathy (fibrinogen, platelets).
What nuclear shape suggests NPM1-mutated AML?
Cuplike nuclei (an invagination of a quarter or more of the nucleus).
Which ELN 2022 group includes TP53 mutation?
Adverse risk.
Which gene fusions define core binding factor AML?
RUNX1::RUNX1T1 [t(8;21)] and CBFB::MYH11 [inv(16)].
Which childhood B-ALL subtypes are favourable?
High hyperdiploidy and ETV6::RUNX1.
What is typical of infant KMT2A-rearranged B-ALL phenotype?
CD10 negative (pro-B), often CD15 positive.
Define ETP-ALL.
T-ALL with CD1a−, CD8−, weak CD5 and at least one stem or myeloid marker (CD34, CD117, HLA-DR, CD13, CD33, CD11b, CD65).
What is the strongest prognostic factor in ALL?
MRD at the end of induction.
Which CML phases does WHO-HAEM5 recognise?
Chronic phase and blast phase (accelerated phase dropped).
What defines CML blast phase?
20% or more blasts in blood or marrow, extramedullary blast proliferation, or increased lymphoblasts (WHO-HAEM5).
What is a major molecular response in CML?
BCR::ABL1 0.1% or less on the International Scale.
What proportion of PV carries JAK2 V617F?
About 95%; most of the rest have JAK2 exon 12 mutations.
Which driver is present in 20–25% of ET?
CALR exon 9 mutation.
What is the minor criterion for PV?
Subnormal serum erythropoietin.
What separates prefibrotic PMF from ET?
Trephine morphology: clustered, atypical megakaryocytes with hypercellularity and granulocytic proliferation in PMF.
Which fusion gene in hypereosinophilia responds to imatinib?
FIP1L1::PDGFRA (and PDGFRB rearrangements).
Which dysplastic feature is most reliable for MDS?
Micromegakaryocytes.
What blast ranges define MDS-IB1 and MDS-IB2?
IB1: 5–9% marrow or 2–4% blood. IB2: 10–19% marrow, 5–19% blood, or Auer rods.
What defines MDS-SF3B1 in WHO-HAEM5?
SF3B1 VAF 5% or more (or 15% ring sideroblasts), low blasts, no del(5q), −7 or complex karyotype.
What is CHIP?
A somatic myeloid mutation at VAF 2% or more with normal blood counts and no haematological neoplasm.
What monocyte count does WHO-HAEM5 need for CMML?
0.5 × 10⁹/L or more and 10% or more of white cells, persistent.
What separates MD-CMML from MP-CMML?
WBC under 13 × 10⁹/L is myelodysplastic; 13 or more is myeloproliferative.
What count separates CLL from MBL?
5 × 10⁹/L clonal B cells with the CLL phenotype.
What does the Matutes score include?
CD5+, CD23+, FMC7−, weak sIg, weak CD22 or CD79b: one point each.
Which test is essential before treating CLL?
TP53 mutation and del(17p) (plus IGHV status).
What phenotype suggests mantle cell lymphoma?
CD5+, CD23− or weak, CD200−, bright sIg; confirm cyclin D1/SOX11 or t(11;14).
Which antigens define hairy cell leukaemia?
CD11c, CD25, CD103, CD123 and annexin A1; BRAF V600E.
Which mutation is found in over 90% of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma?
MYD88 L265P.
What are the SLiM criteria in myeloma?
60% or more clonal plasma cells, FLC ratio 100 or more (involved FLC 100 mg/L or more), more than one MRI focal lesion.
What phenotype separates myeloma from normal plasma cells?
Myeloma: CD19−, CD45− or dim, CD56+, CD27−/CD81−; normal: CD19+, CD45+, CD56−.
Which myeloma translocation predicts venetoclax response?
What defines plasma cell leukaemia now?
5% or more circulating plasma cells.
What phenotype is typical of adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma?
CD4+, CD25 bright, CD7−, HTLV-1 positive.
What phenotype is typical of T-LGL leukaemia?
CD3+, CD8+, CD57+, CD16+, often with STAT3 mutation.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old man with pneumonia has WBC 62 × 10⁹/L with neutrophils, bands and a few myelocytes, toxic granulation and Döhle bodies. Basophils are 0.1 × 10⁹/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.e: Toxic changes, no basophilia and an infective cause point to a leukaemoid reaction. If doubt remains, test BCR::ABL1.

quiz.q: On a CD45/SSC plot, where do myeloblasts usually fall?
o: CD45 dim, SSC low to intermediate
quiz.e: Blasts are CD45 dim with low side scatter: the 'blast gate'. CD45 bright and SSC low is lymphocytes; CD45 negative is erythroid.

quiz.q: Which marker defines T lineage in a mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia?
quiz.e: CD7, CD5 and CD2 are not lineage-specific; strong cytoplasmic or surface CD3 is required.

quiz.q: A marrow has 12% myeloblasts and the karyotype shows inv(16)(p13.1q22). How is it classified?
o: AML with CBFB::MYH11 in both WHO-HAEM5 and ICC
quiz.e: WHO-HAEM5 needs no blast minimum for CBFB::MYH11 and ICC needs 10% or more, so both classify it as AML.

quiz.q: A marrow has 14% blasts, no defining genetic abnormality and an ASXL1 mutation. How does ICC 2022 classify it?
o: MDS/AML with mutated ASXL1 (MR gene mutation)
quiz.e: ICC classifies 10–19% blasts without AML-defining genetics as MDS/AML, qualified by the MR gene mutation. WHO-HAEM5 would call it MDS-IB2.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old woman has bruising, WBC 2.1 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L and blasts with bilobed nuclei and heavy granules. What should happen first?
o: Start ATRA immediately and replace fibrinogen and platelets
quiz.e: Suspected APL is an emergency: early death is from haemorrhage. Start ATRA on morphological suspicion.

quiz.q: Which phenotype is most typical of APL?
quiz.e: APL blasts are characteristically CD34 and HLA-DR negative with bright CD33. Microgranular APL can be CD34 and CD2 positive.

quiz.q: Which B-ALL genetic subtype carries the poorest prognosis?
quiz.e: TCF3::HLF B-ALL has a very poor outcome. High hyperdiploidy, ETV6::RUNX1 and DUX4 are favourable.

quiz.q: A T-ALL is CD1a−, CD8−, CD5 weak in 40% of blasts, CD34+ and CD117+. What is it?
quiz.e: These are the ETP-ALL criteria. It is not MPAL because MPO is not mentioned and CD117 alone does not assign myeloid lineage.

quiz.q: A JAK2 V617F-positive patient has platelets 720 × 10⁹/L, Hb 138 g/L and a trephine with clustered, atypical, hyperchromatic megakaryocytes and grade 1 reticulin. What is the best diagnosis?
quiz.e: Atypical, clustered megakaryocytes with grade 0–1 fibrosis define prefibrotic PMF. ET megakaryocytes are large and hyperlobulated, with no atypia.

quiz.q: In WHO-HAEM5, a CML patient with 12% blasts in the blood is in which phase?
quiz.e: WHO-HAEM5 removed accelerated phase; blast phase needs 20% blasts. ICC would call this accelerated phase.

quiz.q: A marrow shows 7% blasts, multilineage dysplasia and a normal karyotype. Blood blasts are 1%. What is the WHO-HAEM5 diagnosis?
quiz.e: 5–9% marrow blasts is MDS-IB1. ICC would call this MDS with excess blasts.

quiz.q: Which is the most reliable dysplastic feature for MDS?
quiz.e: Micromegakaryocytes are rarely seen outside myeloid neoplasms. Megaloblastoid change also occurs in B12 deficiency.

quiz.q: WBC 15 × 10⁹/L with monocytes 3.2 × 10⁹/L (21%), 2% blood blasts, 6% marrow blasts and no BCR::ABL1. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.e: WBC 13 or more makes it myeloproliferative; blasts under 5% blood and under 10% marrow make it CMML-1.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old has lymphocytes 18 × 10⁹/L, CD5+, CD23+, FMC7−, weak sIgλ and weak CD79b. What is the Matutes score?
quiz.e: All five features score: CD5+, CD23+, FMC7−, weak sIg and weak CD79b. A score of 5 supports CLL.

quiz.q: Clonal B cells are CD5+, CD23−, CD200−, FMC7+ with bright sIg. What test is essential next?
quiz.e: A CD5-positive B-cell neoplasm with a low CLL score must be tested for mantle cell lymphoma.

quiz.q: Pancytopenia, monocytopenia, splenomegaly and a dry tap. Flow shows CD11c+, CD25+, CD103+, CD123 bright B cells. Which mutation is expected?
quiz.e: Classic hairy cell leukaemia carries BRAF V600E in nearly all cases.

quiz.q: A patient has 35% clonal marrow plasma cells, M protein 28 g/L, normal calcium, creatinine and Hb, no bone lesions, and an FLC ratio of 140 (involved 600 mg/L). What is the diagnosis?
quiz.e: An FLC ratio of 100 or more with involved FLC 100 mg/L or more is a SLiM myeloma-defining event, so this is myeloma even without CRAB.

quiz.q: Which phenotype is typical of myeloma plasma cells?
quiz.e: Neoplastic plasma cells typically lose CD19 and CD45 and gain CD56.

quiz.q: A Caribbean-born man has hypercalcaemia, skin lesions and lymphocytes with polylobated 'flower' nuclei that are CD4+ CD25 bright CD7−. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.e: Flower cells, hypercalcaemia and a CD25-bright CD4 phenotype point to HTLV-1-associated ATLL.

steps.q: The film shows a few large cells with bilobed nuclei, heavy granules and one cell with many Auer rods. What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.e: Hypergranular abnormal promyelocytes, a faggot cell and DIC with low fibrinogen are classic for APL.
steps.scene:
A 34-year-old man has 5 days of bruising and bleeding gums. He looks pale.
Hb 82 g/L · WBC 1.8 × 10⁹/L · Platelets 22 × 10⁹/L · PT 19 s · Fibrinogen 0.7 g/L · D-dimer Markedly raised

steps.q: What is the most urgent action?
o: Start ATRA now and give cryoprecipitate and platelets
Insert a central line for chemotherapy
steps.e: Early haemorrhagic death is the main risk. Start ATRA on suspicion, keep fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L and platelets above 30–50 × 10⁹/L, and avoid invasive procedures.

steps.q: Flow cytometry is most likely to show:
o: CD34− HLA-DR− CD33 bright CD117+ MPO strong
steps.e: This is the typical APL phenotype. Confirmation is by PML::RARA (FISH or RT-PCR), which also gives a baseline for molecular MRD.

steps.q: Day 10 of ATRA plus arsenic: he becomes breathless with fever, weight gain and lung infiltrates. What is this?
steps.e:
Differentiation syndrome. Start dexamethasone promptly and consider pausing ATRA or arsenic if severe.
Take-home: APL is an emergency because of coagulopathy, not because of the blast count; Start ATRA on morphology; confirm PML::RARA later; ATRA plus arsenic trioxide cures most low and intermediate-risk patients; Watch for differentiation syndrome and QT prolongation with arsenic.

steps.q: The film shows small, uniform lymphocytes with coarse chromatin and many smudge cells. What is the next test?
steps.e: Peripheral blood flow cytometry is the diagnostic test. A marrow is not needed to diagnose CLL.
steps.scene:
A 71-year-old woman has a routine blood count. She feels well and has no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.
Hb 128 g/L · WBC 24 × 10⁹/L · Lymphocytes 19 × 10⁹/L · Platelets 210 × 10⁹/L

steps.q: Flow shows a κ-restricted B-cell clone that is CD5+, CD23+, CD200+, FMC7−, with weak CD20 and CD79b. What is the diagnosis?
steps.e: Clonal B cells well above 5 × 10⁹/L with a classic phenotype make this CLL. Stage: Binet A / Rai 0.

steps.q: What is the right management now?
o: Watch and wait with regular monitoring
steps.e: Early asymptomatic CLL is monitored. Treat only for active disease (iwCLL criteria): progressive marrow failure, bulky or symptomatic nodes or spleen, rapid doubling time, B symptoms or autoimmune cytopenias not responding to steroids.

steps.q: Two years later she needs treatment. Which test must be done before choosing therapy?
o: TP53 mutation and del(17p) FISH, plus IGHV status
steps.e:
TP53 aberrations predict chemotherapy failure and steer treatment to BTK or BCL2 inhibitors. IGHV status also guides treatment.
Take-home: CLL is diagnosed on blood flow cytometry; Under 5 × 10⁹/L clonal B cells without other features is MBL; Most early CLL needs no treatment; Repeat TP53 testing before every new line of therapy.

steps.q: The film shows neutrophils and myelocytes in two peaks, basophilia and eosinophilia. What is the key diagnostic test?
o: BCR::ABL1 by FISH or RT-PCR (and karyotype)
steps.e: This is the film of CML. Karyotype shows t(9;22) and any additional abnormalities; RT-PCR identifies the transcript type (e13a2/e14a2) for monitoring.
steps.scene:
A 48-year-old man has weight loss and fullness under the left ribs. His spleen is 10 cm below the costal margin.
Hb 112 g/L · WBC 186 × 10⁹/L · Basophils 7 × 10⁹/L · Platelets 640 × 10⁹/L · Blood blasts 3%

steps.q: How does WHO-HAEM5 classify his phase?
o: Cannot be decided without a marrow
steps.e: Blasts are under 20% with no extramedullary blast disease or lymphoblasts, so this is chronic phase. Note the large spleen and basophilia as high-risk features.

steps.q: After 12 months of imatinib, BCR::ABL1 is 0.05% IS. What does this mean?
steps.e:
0.1% IS or lower is a major molecular response, an optimal response at 12 months (ELN).
Take-home: Basophilia and a myelocyte peak point to CML rather than a reaction; WHO-HAEM5 has only chronic and blast phases; Monitor by RT-qPCR on the International Scale; Rising BCR::ABL1: check adherence and ABL1 kinase domain mutations.

steps.q: The blasts are small with scant cytoplasm, no granules and no Auer rods. What is the key next test?
steps.e: Flow cytometry confirms lineage and gives the leukaemia-associated phenotype used later for MRD.
steps.scene:
A 4-year-old boy has 3 weeks of leg pain, pallor and fever. He has a few enlarged neck nodes and a palpable liver and spleen.
Hb 68 g/L · WBC 32 × 10⁹/L · Platelets 18 × 10⁹/L · Blasts (film) 74% · LDH 1100 U/L

steps.q: Blasts are CD19+, CD79a+, cCD22+, CD10+, TdT+, CD34+, MPO−, cCD3−. What is the diagnosis?
steps.e: This is a common (CD10-positive) precursor B-ALL. Burkitt cells are TdT negative with surface light chain.

steps.q: Which genetic finding would most favour a good prognosis?
steps.e: ETV6::RUNX1 and high hyperdiploidy are the favourable childhood subtypes.

steps.q: What is the single most important predictor of outcome after induction?
o: MRD at the end of induction
steps.e:
End-of-induction MRD (flow or IG/TR PCR) guides treatment intensity in modern protocols.
Take-home: Morphology cannot distinguish B-ALL from T-ALL; Hematogones share the B-precursor phenotype but mature in an orderly way; Genetics and MRD together set risk group; Watch for tumour lysis syndrome at diagnosis.

steps.q: The blood film shows marked rouleaux. Which tests best confirm a paraprotein?
o: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains
steps.e: SPEP, immunofixation and serum FLC together detect nearly all myelomas. A urine dipstick misses free light chains.
steps.scene:
A 66-year-old man has 3 months of back pain and tiredness. His GP found kidney impairment.
Hb 92 g/L · Calcium (adj.) 2.9 mmol/L · Creatinine 240 µmol/L · Total protein 98 g/L · ESR 110 mm/h

steps.q: IgG κ paraprotein 46 g/L, κ:λ FLC ratio 85, marrow 38% plasma cells, lytic lesions on whole-body low-dose CT. Does he meet criteria for myeloma?
o: Yes: clonal plasma cells 10% or more plus CRAB features
No, he needs a plasmacytoma biopsy
Only if the FLC ratio is over 100
steps.e: He has hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and bone lesions, any one of which is a myeloma-defining event.

steps.q: Which flow phenotype supports neoplastic plasma cells?
steps.e: Loss of CD19 and CD45 with CD56 gain is typical of myeloma, with a single cytoplasmic light chain.

steps.q: Which FISH result is high-risk?
steps.e:
t(4;14), t(14;16), t(14;20), del(17p) and 1q gain are high-risk. t(11;14) is standard risk but predicts venetoclax response.
Take-home: Rouleaux and a high ESR with renal failure: think myeloma; Use SPEP, immunofixation and serum FLC together; Aspirate plasma cell counts underestimate disease; check CD138 on the trephine; Treat hypercalcaemia and renal impairment urgently.

trees.title: Acute leukaemia lineage
trees.intro: Use once blasts are confirmed. Each question uses flow cytometry or cytochemistry results.

start.q: Is there a defining genetic abnormality (e.g. PML::RARA, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11, NPM1, KMT2A, BCR::ABL1)?

gen.detail: Genetics take priority, for example 'AML with NPM1 mutation' or 'MPAL with BCR::ABL1'. Check the blast threshold for each system (WHO-HAEM5 or ICC).

mpo.q: Is MPO positive (cytochemistry or flow), or are Auer rods present?

mpo2.q: Do the blasts also meet T criteria (strong cCD3) or B criteria (strong CD19 with CD79a, cCD22 or CD10)?

mpal.detail: MPAL B/myeloid or T/myeloid. Exclude AML with a defining genetic lesion and CML in blast phase first.

aml.detail: Classify by genetics (karyotype, FISH, NGS: NPM1, FLT3, CEBPA, TP53, MR genes), otherwise by differentiation.

mono.q: Monocytic markers: two or more of NSE, CD11c, CD14, CD64, lysozyme?

monoaml.detail: Acute monocytic or myelomonocytic leukaemia. Count promonocytes as blasts. Check KMT2A and NPM1.

tall.q: Is it CD1a−, CD8−, CD5 weak, with CD34, CD117, HLA-DR, CD13, CD33, CD11b or CD65?

etp.detail: ETP-ALL. Often has myeloid-type mutations (FLT3, RAS, DNMT3A). Watch MRD closely.

tall2.detail: Stage by CD1a, surface CD3, CD4 and CD8. Image the mediastinum.

cd19.q: Is CD19 positive with CD79a, cCD22 or CD10?

ball.q: Is TdT or CD34 positive, with no surface light chain?
opts: No: TdT− with surface light chain

ball2.detail: Send karyotype, FISH (BCR::ABL1, KMT2A, ETV6::RUNX1, iAMP21) and ploidy. Exclude hematogones by maturation pattern.

burkitt.detail: Check MYC rearrangement, Ki-67, BCL2. Not ALL: treat as Burkitt lymphoma.

other.q: Do the blasts express CD41/CD61 or CD71/CD235a?

mk.detail: Consider Down syndrome, RBM15::MRTFA (infants) and CML blast phase. A trephine may be needed (fibrosis).

ery.detail: WHO-HAEM5: erythroid cells 80% or more with 30% or more proerythroblasts. Usually TP53 mutated, very poor prognosis.

aul.detail: No lineage-specific markers. Exclude rare entities (blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm: CD123, CD4, CD56, TCF4).

trees.title: Mature B-cell phenotype
trees.intro: Use for a clonal (light chain-restricted) B-cell population in blood or marrow.

cd5.q: Matutes score (CD5+, CD23+, FMC7−, weak sIg, weak CD79b/CD22)?

cll.q: Are clonal B cells 5 × 10⁹/L or more, or are there nodes, organomegaly or cytopenias?

cll2.detail: Stage (Binet or Rai). Before treatment: TP53 mutation, del(17p), IGHV status.

mbl.detail: Low-count (under 0.5 × 10⁹/L) or CLL-type MBL. Repeat counts; progression to CLL is about 1–2% a year.

mcl.end: Probable mantle cell lymphoma: test cyclin D1/SOX11 or t(11;14)
mcl.detail: CD200 negative and bright sIg support MCL. If cyclin D1 negative, consider atypical CLL or CD5+ marginal zone lymphoma.

gcb.q: Very high proliferation, vacuolated blue cells, BCL2 negative?

bl.detail: Confirm MYC rearrangement without BCL2. An emergency: tumour lysis risk.

fl.end: Follicular lymphoma (or another germinal centre lymphoma)
fl.detail: Cleaved cells; BCL2+, BCL6+. FISH for IGH::BCL2. Exclude DLBCL in the leukaemic phase.

hcl.q: Are CD11c, CD25, CD103 and CD123 all positive?

hcl2.detail: Confirm BRAF V600E and annexin A1 on the trephine. Monocytopenia is typical.

lpl.detail: Test MYD88 L265P and CXCR4. Watch for hyperviscosity.

mzl2.end: Marginal zone lymphoma (splenic) or other small B-cell lymphoma
mzl2.detail: Villous lymphocytes and splenomegaly favour splenic MZL. Prominent nucleoli and CD25−, BRAF wild type: splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukaemia with prominent nucleoli.

check.title: Reporting a suspected leukaemia
check.intro: A systematic order for the first day of a suspected haematological neoplasm. Tick each step as you go.
steps: Confirm the count and the film
Repeat the count if needed, check for platelet clumps and smudge cells, and do a 200-cell differential.
Count blasts and blast equivalents
Include promonocytes, and abnormal promyelocytes in APL. Note Auer rods.
Look for an emergency
APL features or DIC, hyperleucocytosis (leucostasis), tumour lysis, hypercalcaemia. Phone the clinical team.
Describe dysplasia and lineage clues
Hypogranular or pseudo-Pelger neutrophils, micromegakaryocytes, monocytic features, basophilia.
Send flow cytometry
Blood is often enough; use marrow if blasts are few. Ask for a lineage panel or a B/T lymphoproliferative panel.
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine
500-cell differential, Perls stain, reticulin; send samples for karyotype, FISH and molecular testing in the right media.
Genetics
Karyotype; FISH or RT-PCR for urgent fusions (PML::RARA, BCR::ABL1); NGS myeloid or lymphoid panel (NPM1, FLT3, CEBPA, TP53, MR genes).
Integrated report
Name the entity in WHO-HAEM5 and ICC terms, note blast percentage, phenotype, genetics pending, and any qualifiers (post-cytotoxic therapy, germline).

title: Haemostasis
facts: Which receptor binds VWF during platelet adhesion?
GPIb–IX–V.
Which receptor mediates platelet aggregation?
GPIIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3), binding fibrinogen and VWF.
What does aspirin inhibit?
COX-1, blocking thromboxane A2 synthesis for the platelet's lifetime.
What are the three phases of the cell-based model?
Initiation, amplification and propagation.
Which factors does the PT test?
VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen.
Which factors does the APTT test?
XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen (and prekallikrein, HMWK).
Which factor deficiency prolongs the APTT without bleeding?
Factor XII (also prekallikrein and HMWK).
Which vitamin K-dependent factor has the shortest half-life?
Factor VII (about 6 hours).
What is the correct citrate tube and ratio?
3.2% sodium citrate, 9 parts blood to 1 part citrate, filled at least 90%.
How is citrate adjusted for a high haematocrit?
Citrate (mL) = 0.00185 × blood volume (mL) × (100 − Hct%), when Hct is over 0.55.
What does a mixing study that corrects suggest?
A factor deficiency.
Why incubate an APTT mix for 1–2 hours?
Acquired FVIII inhibitors are time- and temperature-dependent.
How is the INR calculated?
(Patient PT ÷ mean normal PT) raised to the power of the ISI.
What causes pseudothrombocytopenia?
EDTA-dependent antiplatelet antibodies causing clumps or satellitism.
What ADAMTS13 level supports TTP?
Below 10%.
What is the first treatment for suspected TTP?
Urgent plasma exchange (with steroids; caplacizumab and rituximab).
What does the PLASMIC score include?
Platelets under 30, haemolysis, no active cancer, no transplant, MCV under 90 fL, INR under 1.5, creatinine under 2 mg/dL.
What are the 4Ts?
Thrombocytopenia, Timing, Thrombosis, oTher causes.
When does HIT usually start?
5–10 days after starting heparin (within a day if heparin was given in the previous 100 days).
Why avoid warfarin in acute HIT?
It lowers protein C and can cause venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis.
Which inherited thrombocytopenia has small platelets?
Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome.
Which disorder has giant platelets and Döhle-like inclusions?
MYH9-related disorders (May–Hegglin anomaly).
What VWF level confirms VWD regardless of bleeding?
Below 30 IU/dL (ASH/ISTH 2021).
What ratio suggests type 2 VWD?
VWF activity to antigen ratio under 0.7.
Which VWD type mimics mild haemophilia A?
Type 2N (defective FVIII binding).
Which VWD type shows enhanced RIPA at low ristocetin?
Type 2B (and platelet-type pseudo-VWD).
Why avoid DDAVP in type 2B VWD?
It releases abnormal VWF and worsens thrombocytopenia.
Which blood group has lower VWF?
Group O, about 25% lower.
What is Heyde syndrome?
Aortic stenosis with GI bleeding from angiodysplasia and acquired VWD (loss of HMW multimers).
Which platelet disorder fails to aggregate with all agonists except ristocetin?
Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb/IIIa defect).
What defines severe haemophilia?
Factor level below 1 IU/dL.
What is a Bethesda unit?
The amount of inhibitor that neutralises 50% of the factor in normal plasma.
How does emicizumab affect the APTT?
It shortens the APTT to normal; one-stage FVIII and Bethesda assays become invalid.
Which deficiency bleeds with normal PT and APTT?
Factor XIII (also VWD, platelet disorders, mild factor deficiencies).
What is the ISTH overt DIC score threshold?
5 or more.
What is the commonest cause of DIC?
Sepsis.
What fibrinogen level predicts severe postpartum haemorrhage?
Below 2 g/L.
How is the D-dimer cut-off age-adjusted?
Age × 10 µg/L FEU for patients over 50.
What does factor V Leiden cause?
Resistance to activated protein C.
Which natural anticoagulant deficiency carries the highest VTE risk?
Antithrombin deficiency.
When should protein C and S not be tested?
During acute thrombosis, on warfarin, in pregnancy (PS) or liver disease.
What laboratory criteria define APS?
Persistent LA, aCL or anti-β2GPI on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart.
Which two tests are used for lupus anticoagulant?
dRVVT and an LA-sensitive APTT, each with screen, mix and confirm.
What is the UFH anti-Xa target?
When is LMWH anti-Xa measured?
3–4 hours after a dose.
What reverses dabigatran?
Idarucizumab.
What reverses warfarin in major bleeding?
IV vitamin K and four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate.
What does a normal thrombin time tell you about dabigatran?
Clinically significant dabigatran is unlikely.

quiz.q: A patient has PT 11 s (normal), APTT 62 s (long). The 1:1 mix corrects immediately and after 2 hours of incubation. Which is most likely?
quiz.e: Correction immediately and after incubation suggests a deficiency of an intrinsic factor. LA and heparin do not correct; acquired FVIII inhibitors fail to correct after incubation.

quiz.q: Which result pattern fits factor VII deficiency?
quiz.e: Factor VII is tested only by the PT.

quiz.q: A sample has haematocrit 0.65. What happens if the standard citrate tube is used?
quiz.e: Less plasma means relatively too much citrate, which binds the calcium added in the test and prolongs clotting times.

quiz.q: Platelets 32 × 10⁹/L on an analyser; the film shows large platelet aggregates at the feathered edge. What is the next step?
o: Repeat the count on a citrate sample
quiz.e: Clumps suggest EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia. Repeat in citrate and correct for dilution.

quiz.q: A 35-year-old woman has confusion, Hb 78 g/L, platelets 14 × 10⁹/L, many schistocytes, LDH 1800 U/L, normal PT, and negative DAT. What is the immediate management?
quiz.e: This is probable TTP. Start plasma exchange without waiting for ADAMTS13; platelet transfusion is avoided unless there is life-threatening bleeding.

quiz.q: Day 7 after hip surgery on prophylactic heparin, platelets fall from 280 to 95 × 10⁹/L and a DVT is found. No other cause. What is the 4Ts score?
quiz.e: Fall over 50% with nadir 20 or more (2), day 5–10 onset (2), new thrombosis (2), no other cause (2): 8, high probability.

quiz.q: In suspected HIT with an intermediate 4Ts score, what should be done?
o: Continue heparin and wait for the antibody test
Stop heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant
quiz.e: Stop all heparin, start argatroban, fondaparinux, bivalirudin or a DOAC, and send the anti-PF4 immunoassay.

quiz.q: VWF:Ag 52 IU/dL, VWF activity (GPIbM) 18 IU/dL, FVIII 48 IU/dL, absent high-molecular-weight multimers, normal RIPA at low ristocetin. Which type?
quiz.e: Activity/antigen ratio 0.35 with loss of HMW multimers and no enhanced RIPA indicates type 2A.

quiz.q: Which finding most suggests type 2B VWD?
o: Enhanced agglutination at low-dose ristocetin with thrombocytopenia
quiz.e: Gain-of-function VWF binds GPIb spontaneously, clearing platelets and HMW multimers.

quiz.q: Platelet aggregation is absent with ADP, collagen, adrenaline and arachidonic acid, but normal with ristocetin. Count and size are normal. Diagnosis?
quiz.e: Glanzmann thrombasthenia lacks GPIIb/IIIa, so fibrinogen-dependent aggregation fails; ristocetin agglutination needs only VWF and GPIb.

quiz.q: A boy has FVIII 0.6 IU/dL. How is his haemophilia classified?
quiz.e: Below 1 IU/dL is severe haemophilia.

quiz.q: A haemophilia A patient on emicizumab has an APTT of 28 s (normal). What does this mean?
o: Emicizumab has normalised the APTT; it does not reflect haemostatic protection
quiz.e: Emicizumab shortens APTT-based tests; use chromogenic assays with bovine reagents for FVIII or inhibitors.

quiz.q: A 78-year-old woman has large spontaneous bruises, Hb 84 g/L, normal PT and platelets, APTT 74 s that corrects immediately but prolongs after 2 hours of incubation. Diagnosis?
quiz.e: A time-dependent inhibitor in an older adult with extensive bleeding is acquired haemophilia A. Measure FVIII and the Bethesda titre.

quiz.q: Which deficiency causes umbilical stump bleeding with normal PT and APTT?
quiz.e: Factor XIII cross-links fibrin and is not tested by routine clotting screens.

quiz.q: A septic patient has platelets 42 × 10⁹/L, PT prolonged by 5 s, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L and a strongly raised D-dimer. What is the ISTH DIC score?
quiz.e: Platelets under 50 (2), strong D-dimer rise (3), PT 3–6 s (1), fibrinogen under 1 (1): 7, overt DIC.

quiz.q: Which test is unreliable for diagnosing VTE in a hospitalised patient with high clinical probability?
quiz.e: D-dimer is only useful to exclude VTE when probability is low; it is often raised in inpatients.

quiz.q: Which thrombophilia test is valid during warfarin therapy?
quiz.e: Genetic tests are unaffected by anticoagulants. Warfarin lowers protein C and S and interferes with LA testing.

quiz.q: Which combination confirms the laboratory criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome?
o: One positive LA during acute thrombosis
quiz.e: Antibodies must persist on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart, ideally tested off anticoagulation.

quiz.q: A patient on apixaban needs urgent surgery. Which test best measures the drug level?
quiz.e: PT and APTT are insensitive to apixaban; use a drug-calibrated anti-Xa assay.

quiz.q: Warfarin patient, INR 9.2, intracranial bleed. What is the correct reversal?
o: IV vitamin K and four-factor PCC
quiz.e: Major bleeding needs immediate PCC plus IV vitamin K to sustain the effect.

steps.q: The film shows many schistocytes. Which test best supports the haemolysis being microangiopathic rather than immune?
steps.e: A negative DAT with schistocytes and thrombocytopenia defines MAHA. Normal clotting tests argue against DIC.
steps.scene:
A 38-year-old woman has 2 days of headache, confusion and bruising. Temperature 37.9 °C.
Hb 72 g/L · Platelets 11 × 10⁹/L · Retics 8% · LDH 2100 U/L · Creatinine 118 µmol/L · PT / APTT Normal

steps.q: Her PLASMIC score is 7. What should happen now?
o: Urgent plasma exchange and steroids, before ADAMTS13 returns
steps.e: A high PLASMIC score means a high probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. Delay in plasma exchange increases mortality.

steps.q: ADAMTS13 activity is under 5% with an inhibitor. What else is now standard therapy?
steps.e:
Caplacizumab blocks VWF–GPIb binding and shortens time to platelet recovery; rituximab reduces relapse.
Take-home: MAHA plus thrombocytopenia is TTP until proven otherwise; Do not wait for ADAMTS13 before plasma exchange; Avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding; Monitor ADAMTS13 in remission to predict relapse.

steps.q: What is his 4Ts score?
steps.e: Fall of 68% with nadir 84 (2), onset day 8 (2), new thrombosis (2), no other cause (2): 8.
steps.scene:
A 66-year-old man had a knee replacement 8 days ago and is on prophylactic LMWH. His calf is swollen today.
Platelets (day 0) 265 × 10⁹/L · Platelets (day 8) 84 × 10⁹/L · Ultrasound Proximal DVT · Other causes None found

steps.q: What is the immediate management?
o: Stop LMWH and start argatroban or fondaparinux
steps.e: Stop all heparin, including flushes, and give a non-heparin anticoagulant at therapeutic dose.

steps.q: The anti-PF4 immunoassay is strongly positive. What confirms clinically important antibodies?
o: A functional assay such as SRA or HIPA
steps.e:
Functional assays show that the antibodies activate platelets; a high immunoassay optical density also raises the likelihood.
Take-home: HIT causes thrombosis, not bleeding; Use the 4Ts before testing; Warfarin only after platelet recovery, overlapping with a non-heparin agent; Record heparin allergy prominently.

steps.q: Which tests are the best first step?
o: VWF antigen, VWF activity and FVIII
steps.e: Mucocutaneous bleeding with a mildly long APTT suggests VWD; measure VWF:Ag, activity and FVIII together.
steps.scene:
A 19-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding, frequent nosebleeds and prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction. Her mother bruises easily.
Platelets 256 × 10⁹/L · PT 12 s · APTT 38 s (ref 26–36) · Blood group O · ISTH-BAT score 9

steps.q: VWF:Ag 26 IU/dL, activity 24 IU/dL, FVIII 34 IU/dL, normal multimers. What is the diagnosis?
steps.e: Proportionate reduction below 30 IU/dL with normal multimers is type 1 VWD; blood group O does not explain levels this low.

steps.q: What is the best plan for future dental extraction?
o: DDAVP trial now; then DDAVP plus tranexamic acid for procedures
steps.e:
Most type 1 patients respond to desmopressin; confirm the response with a trial. Tranexamic acid helps mucosal bleeding.
Take-home: Use a bleeding assessment tool; Repeat borderline VWF levels; stress and oestrogens raise them; Test VWF activity/antigen ratio to look for type 2; Heavy menstrual bleeding is often the main symptom.

cases.title: A swollen knee in a toddler

steps.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.e: Haemarthrosis in a boy with an isolated very long APTT and a maternal family history points to haemophilia.
steps.scene:
A 14-month-old boy, just walking, has a hot swollen knee after a minor fall. His maternal uncle had 'bleeding problems'.
Platelets 310 × 10⁹/L · PT 12 s · APTT 88 s · Fibrinogen 2.8 g/L

steps.q: FVIII is under 1 IU/dL. After 20 exposures to recombinant FVIII, bleeds stop responding. What should be tested?
o: Bethesda assay for an FVIII inhibitor
steps.e: Inhibitors usually develop in the first 50 exposure days. Measure the titre with the Nijmegen–Bethesda assay.

steps.q: He is started on emicizumab. His APTT is now 27 s. How should FVIII be measured in future?
steps.e:
Emicizumab interferes with APTT-based assays; bovine chromogenic assays are not affected.
Take-home: Haemophilia is X-linked; test female carriers; Severity is set by the factor level; Inhibitors: Bethesda assay; bypassing agents or emicizumab; Know which assays emicizumab invalidates.

steps.q: What is her ISTH overt DIC score?
steps.e: Platelets under 50 (2), strong D-dimer (3), PT over 6 s prolonged (2), fibrinogen under 1 g/L (1): 8.
steps.scene:
A 31-year-old woman has a placental abruption with intrauterine death and is now bleeding from venepuncture sites.
Hb 68 g/L · Platelets 48 × 10⁹/L · PT 19 s (ref 11–14) · APTT 52 s · Fibrinogen 0.8 g/L · D-dimer Very high

steps.q: Which blood component is the priority?
o: Fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate to raise fibrinogen above 2 g/L
steps.e: Low fibrinogen is the strongest predictor of severe postpartum bleeding; replace early along with red cells, plasma and platelets.

steps.q: What else should be given early in obstetric haemorrhage?
steps.e:
Tranexamic acid within 3 hours reduces death from postpartum haemorrhage (WOMAN trial).
Take-home: DIC is always secondary; deliver and treat the cause; Fibrinogen falls early in obstetric DIC; Use serial counts and fibrinogen to guide replacement; Viscoelastic testing can guide transfusion.

trees.title: Abnormal clotting screen
trees.intro: Start with a PT and APTT from a correctly filled citrate sample, with no heparin contamination.

pt.q: Is the patient on warfarin, malnourished, on antibiotics, or jaundiced?

vitk.end: Early warfarin effect, vitamin K deficiency or liver disease
vitk.detail: Factor VII falls first. Give vitamin K if deficient; check liver function.

f7.detail: Assay factor VII. Mild deficiency is common and often asymptomatic.

aptt.q: Is heparin possible (line sample, treatment)? Is the TT long?

hep.detail: Repeat from a fresh venepuncture, or neutralise heparin (heparinase) and repeat.

mix.q: 1:1 mixing study: does it correct, immediately and after 2 hours at 37 °C?

deficiency.q: Does the patient have a bleeding history?

factors.end: Factor VIII, IX or XI deficiency, or VWD
factors.detail: Assay FVIII, FIX, FXI and VWF (antigen and activity). In a male child with joint bleeds, think haemophilia.

f12.end: Probable factor XII (or prekallikrein, HMWK) deficiency
f12.detail: Assay FXII. No bleeding risk; procedures can go ahead.

acqh.detail: Urgent: low FVIII, Bethesda titre. Bypassing agents for bleeding; immunosuppression.

la.q: Is the dRVVT or LA-sensitive APTT confirm step positive?

laa.detail: Thrombotic, not haemorrhagic. Repeat after 12 weeks with aCL and anti-β2GPI.

inh.detail: Assay factors at several dilutions; Bethesda assay for the affected factor.

both.q: Are platelets low and D-dimer high, with low fibrinogen?

dic.detail: Calculate the ISTH score; treat the cause; replace for bleeding.

both2.q: Is the patient on warfarin or a DOAC, or has liver disease or vitamin K deficiency?

drug.end: Drug effect, liver disease or vitamin K deficiency
drug.detail: Check INR, drug levels (anti-Xa, dTT) and liver tests. Factor V is normal in vitamin K deficiency and low in liver disease.

common.end: Common pathway deficiency (X, V, II) or fibrinogen disorder
common.detail: Assay factors X, V and II and Clauss fibrinogen (with antigen for dysfibrinogenaemia). Consider amyloidosis (acquired factor X deficiency).

none.q: Is the bleeding mucocutaneous (nose, gums, menstrual, bruising)?

muco.detail: VWF:Ag, activity, FVIII; film and platelet size; PFA-100 and aggregometry. Check drugs (aspirin, SSRIs).

deep.end: Check factor XIII and mild factor deficiencies
deep.detail: FXIII assay, FVIII, FIX, FXI, fibrinogen; consider hyperfibrinolysis (α2-antiplasmin, PAI-1).

trees.title: Thrombocytopenia
trees.intro: Use for a platelet count under 150 × 10⁹/L.

start.q: Does the film show platelet clumps or satellitism?

pseudo.detail: Repeat in citrate (× 1.1) and report the corrected count.

maha.q: Are there schistocytes with haemolysis (high LDH, low haptoglobin)?

tma.q: Are PT, APTT and fibrinogen normal?

ttp.end: Thrombotic microangiopathy: TTP until proven otherwise
ttp.detail: PLASMIC score, ADAMTS13, urgent plasma exchange. Stool for STEC in diarrhoea (HUS).

hep.q: Has the patient received heparin in the last 100 days?

hit.detail: Intermediate or high: stop heparin, non-heparin anticoagulant, anti-PF4 assay.

other.q: Are the other blood counts or the film abnormal (blasts, dysplasia, leucoerythroblastic)?

marrow.detail: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine: leukaemia, MDS, aplasia, infiltration, megaloblastic anaemia.

iso.q: Is there splenomegaly, liver disease or pregnancy?

spleen.detail: Usually moderate thrombocytopenia; check portal hypertension.

preg.detail: Gestational: over 70 × 10⁹/L in late pregnancy. Check BP, liver enzymes, LDH.

itp.q: Are platelets large, or the family affected from childhood?

inh.detail: Platelet size, neutrophil inclusions (MYH9), flow for GPIb/GPIIb-IIIa, gene panel.

itp2.detail: Check drugs, HIV, HCV, H. pylori, thyroid; DAT; treat if bleeding or very low.

check.title: Coagulation sample checks
check.intro: Check these before releasing an abnormal coagulation result. Tick each step as you go.
steps: Right tube and fill
3.2% citrate, 9:1, filled at least 90%. Underfilling prolongs results.
Haematocrit
If Hct is over 0.55, request a new sample with adjusted citrate.
Clots and haemolysis
A clotted sample shortens or prolongs results and lowers fibrinogen and platelets. Reject it.
Heparin contamination
Line samples, a very long APTT and TT. Repeat from a clean venepuncture.
Timing and storage
PT within 24 h, APTT within 4 h; freeze plasma for specialist tests (double-centrifuged, platelet-poor).
Anticoagulant history
Warfarin, heparin, DOACs, emicizumab: record the drug, dose and time of last dose.
Interpret the pattern
PT, APTT, TT, fibrinogen and platelets together; decide on mixing study or factor assays.
Phone critical results
Fibrinogen under 1 g/L, INR over 5 (or local limit), unexpected very long APTT, platelets under 20 × 10⁹/L, suspected TTP or HIT.
